assessment.nobel_worthiness: Credit Cycles (1997) showed how collateral constraints interact with asset prices to amplify and propagate shocks. It became the workhorse for macro-financial models. It underlies much of modern thinking on financial crises and balance-sheet channels, and it has been extended widely in macro, finance and policy analysis.
assessment.attribution: The core mechanism is clearly the joint work of Kiyotaki and Moore. Gertler and Gilchrist belong to the adjacent financial-accelerator line, which overlaps with work already recognised in 2022, so the proposal is limited to the two originators.
assessment.maturity: Nearly three decades of citation, extension, quantitative use and empirical testing after the 2007-09 crisis. The idea is well confirmed and the timing is ripe.
uncertainties: Possible overlap with the 2022 prize on banks and crises could weigh against it.
Empirical identification of collateral-driven amplification is less settled than the theory.
My knowledge of recent citation trends is imperfect.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The Redux model and the Foundations of International Macroeconomics created the intertemporal microfounded framework for open-economy macro. They also framed the exchange-rate disconnect puzzles that organise the field. The framework is central to teaching and to policy analysis in central banks and international institutions.
assessment.attribution: Obstfeld and Rogoff are the natural joint pair for the framework and for the puzzles. Rogoff's separate crisis-history work with Reinhart is a distinct ballot entry and is not needed for this proposal.
assessment.maturity: More than 25 years of use, with a durable and well-tested framework. The field has had no recent recognition, so the timing is appropriate.
uncertainties: Some of the puzzles remain unresolved, which some members might read as incompleteness.
Weighing this against the other macro entries, especially New Keynesian and macro-finance, is a judgement call.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Grossman and Helpman produced two large bodies of work. One is endogenous-growth models of innovation in the global economy. The other is the political-economy theory of trade protection (Protection for Sale), which has been widely tested. Together they changed how economists think about trade policy, growth and the role of interest groups.
assessment.attribution: The contributions are jointly authored in books and papers, and the pair is the unambiguous core. Helpman also appears in the firm-heterogeneity entry, and I credit that work separately.
assessment.maturity: Work from the late 1980s to the 1990s, with decades of empirical and theoretical follow-up. The trade field has only the 2008 recognition on a different theme.
uncertainties: Some members may prefer the firm-heterogeneity line (Melitz) as the more consequential trade advance.
Empirical support for the political-economy models is mixed.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Berry-Levinsohn-Pakes (BLP) demand estimation with differentiated products, together with Pakes's work on dynamic industry models, became the standard empirical toolkit in industrial organisation. It is also used in antitrust, merger review and trade. This is an unusually strong case of a method that changed practice across applied fields.
assessment.attribution: The 1995 BLP paper makes the three-person core clear. Pakes has the broader dynamic-model portfolio, so one could argue for a narrower pair. Bresnahan, Reiss, Benkard and Levin are important but more peripheral to this specific contribution.
assessment.maturity: Thirty years of dominant use. The contribution is firmly established.
uncertainties: The three-name limit forces exclusion of other major contributors such as Bresnahan.
Attribution between demand-side and dynamic-model contributions is debatable.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Nominal rigidities, Calvo pricing, Taylor rules and the microfounded New Keynesian synthesis underpin modern monetary policy analysis in central banks. Practical impact is very large and the intellectual influence is deep.
assessment.attribution: This is the hardest attribution on the list. Many people contributed to the framework (Gali, Gertler, Christiano, Eichenbaum, Smets and others). The selected trio covers the staggered-price and wage mechanism, the policy rule and the theoretical synthesis. Reasonable alternative trios exist.
assessment.maturity: Fully mature and tested through several decades of policy use. The post-2021 inflation episode has given the framework a further real-world test, with mixed results.
uncertainties: Attribution is contested and may make consensus difficult.
The framework's performance during the recent inflation surge is debated.
Part of the area overlaps with work already recognised in earlier macro prizes.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Hsieh and Klenow (2009) quantified how misallocation of inputs across firms can explain a large share of cross-country TFP differences. It opened a large literature linking micro-level distortions to aggregate income gaps and development. It has been very influential in macro, growth and development.
assessment.attribution: Hsieh and Klenow are the central pair for the measurement framework. Restuccia and Rogerson are closely related but are not listed together with them here.
assessment.maturity: About 15 years of impact, with extensive replication and critiques of measurement. It is somewhat younger than the other leading entries.
uncertainties: Measurement error and the interpretation of dispersion as distortion remain debated.
The contribution may be viewed as less mature than longer-established frameworks.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: This work moved adverse selection from theory to credible measurement in real insurance markets. It used designs with administrative data and quantified welfare costs and policy implications. It also shaped health-insurance policy debate.
assessment.attribution: Finkelstein and Einav are the leading joint contributors. Salanie contributes important theory and econometrics, but I limit the proposal to the two most associated with the empirical research programme.
assessment.maturity: Roughly 15 to 20 years of work with substantial replication. It is still developing, and the case may strengthen with time.
uncertainties: The contribution may be seen as early relative to more established candidates.
Selecting among the three names is uncertain.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: This work used tax records to build long-run series on top incomes and wealth. It reshaped the empirical and policy debate on inequality and showed how much income and wealth are concentrated. Its influence on research and public debate is very large, and the data construction is a lasting contribution.
assessment.attribution: The three form a coherent research group. Credit for the data programme is shared with Atkinson, who is deceased, and with others. The theoretical claims in Piketty's synthesis are more contested than the measurement contribution.
assessment.maturity: More than 20 years of empirical work, with active methodological debate about data construction and about the distributional national accounts.
uncertainties: Measurement disputes and the contested interpretation of capital dynamics could weigh against it.
The three-person fit and the weight on theory versus data are unclear.
The area is near my own research interests (inequality and macro), which I disclose.
